explanation: Ocular ischemic syndrome is the unifying diagnosis: pain, dilated but non-tortuous veins, mid-peripheral hemorrhages, corneal edema and rubeosis in one eye of an elderly vasculopath, while the fellow eye shows only mild background diabetic change. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is a bilateral, roughly symmetric disease, so a fellow eye with only scattered microaneurysms argues strongly against it. Branch retinal vein occlusion produces a sectoral, wedge-shaped hemorrhage pattern respecting the horizontal raphe and is rarely painful or associated with rubeosis of this degree. The combination of ocular pain (from ischemia and raised pressure) with marked interocular asymmetry is the classic examination-room signature of carotid occlusive disease.

CMV retinitis is monitored by serially documenting the leading border of the necrotic lesion, because progression is defined as advancement of that edge; imaging the edge of active retinitis is therefore the correct monitoring strategy. Serial photographs of vitritis are useless because immunosuppressed patients with low CD4 counts mount little vitreous inflammation, and the vitreous haze does not track disease activity. Fluorescein angiography adds nothing beyond what is visible clinically and exposes the patient to unnecessary dye. The nuance worth teaching is that the historical gold standard is serial wide-field colour fundus photography of the lesion border; autofluorescence of the border is a modern adjunct that highlights the transition from active necrosis to atrophic scar.

The inflammation has worsened from 3+ to 4+ cells despite prednisolone every four hours, so the steroid must be intensified rather than tapered; under-treated uveitis is itself a cause of trabeculitis and secondary pressure elevation. The pressure remains above target at 28 mmHg, so an aqueous suppressant is added, and timolol is the appropriate choice. Prostaglandin analogues such as latanoprost are relatively contraindicated in active uveitis because they can aggravate intraocular inflammation and promote cystoid macular oedema. Both options that reduce prednisolone to once daily would allow the uveitis to escalate further, which is exactly the wrong direction given a rising cell count.

The narrative is diagnostic: blunt trauma, then months of pressure around 5 mmHg, which points to a cyclodialysis cleft allowing direct suprachoroidal outflow and suppressed aqueous production. When such a cleft closes, either spontaneously or after treatment, the eye abruptly regains its aqueous load against an outflow system that has been dormant, producing a dramatic and often painful pressure spike into the fifties. Ghost cell glaucoma follows a vitreous haemorrhage by weeks, presents with khaki-coloured cells in the anterior chamber, and would not be preceded by months of hypotony. Angle recession glaucoma develops insidiously over years with a gradually rising pressure and never explains the preceding prolonged hypotony.

In an eye harbouring a uveal melanoma, filtering procedures and tube shunts create a direct transscleral conduit and are avoided because of the theoretical risk of seeding tumour cells into the subconjunctival space and orbit. Transscleral cyclophotocoagulation lowers pressure without creating such a fistula, which makes it the preferred surgical option once maximal medical therapy has failed. Simply observing on full medical therapy is not acceptable when the pressure remains uncontrolled, since the eye still has useful vision at 20/100 and the nerve is at risk. The usual sequence in practice is to treat any underlying radiation-induced neovascular component with anti-VEGF and panretinal photocoagulation first, then proceed to cyclodestruction if the pressure remains high.

Recurrent unilateral episodes of markedly raised pressure with stellate keratic precipitates, corneal oedema and minimal cell describe glaucomatocyclitic crisis, and the immediate threat to the eye in the emergency room is the pressure itself. Aqueous suppressants, with a topical beta blocker as the standard first agent, act fastest to protect the optic nerve and clear the epithelial oedema. Topical steroid is certainly part of definitive management and is usually started at the same visit, but it does not lower pressure acutely and its benefit accrues over days. Prostaglandins and miotics are avoided in this inflammatory setting, and the question is asking specifically what is most important to institute first.

When pressure stays high after a peripheral iridotomy the first obligation is to prove the iridotomy is actually patent and of adequate size, best confirmed by transillumination and by seeing the anterior capsule through it; a pigment-plugged or incomplete iridotomy is the commonest reason for apparent failure. Only once patency is confirmed should you go on to consider non-pupillary-block mechanisms such as plateau iris configuration, residual peripheral anterior synechiae, or a lens-related component. A mild cataract by definition is not phacomorphic, so lens extraction on that indication is not justified at this point. Reaching for phacoemulsification before verifying the simplest and most reversible cause is poor surgical judgement.

This is neovascular glaucoma after central retinal vein occlusion in an eye whose visual potential is hand motions and whose dense cataract and corneal oedema make retinal laser physically impossible. Cyclophotocoagulation lowers pressure and relieves pain without requiring a clear view, and is the standard choice for an uncontrolled neovascular eye with poor visual prognosis. Panretinal photocoagulation is the correct treatment in principle but cannot be delivered through this media, and topical medication alone will not control pressure once the angle is closed by a fibrovascular membrane. Retrobulbar alcohol is reserved for a blind, painful eye as a purely palliative measure, not for an eye still perceiving hand motions. In current practice intravitreal anti-VEGF is given alongside to regress the neovascularisation while the cyclodestruction controls pressure.

Pressure elevation appearing roughly four to twelve weeks after a glaucoma drainage device is the classic hypertensive phase, caused by a fibrous capsule maturing around the extraocular plate and increasing resistance to aqueous absorption. It is most often seen with valved implants once the plate has been exposed to aqueous for several weeks. Steroid response would typically appear earlier and is diagnosed by the temporal relationship to intensive topical steroid, and persistent inflammation would be accompanied by visible cell and flare. Progressive glaucoma describes worsening optic neuropathy over years and does not explain an abrupt pressure rise at eight weeks in an eye with a functioning drain.

In a shallow-chamber, high-pressure eye after phacoemulsification with endocyclophotocoagulation the differential is pupillary block, suprachoroidal haemorrhage or effusion, and aqueous misdirection. B-scan is genuinely useful here because it excludes a suprachoroidal haemorrhage or effusion, and ultrasound biomicroscopy is the test that demonstrates anteriorly rotated ciliary processes with the lens-iris diaphragm pushed forward. Confirming iridotomy patency is likewise essential, since aqueous misdirection can only be diagnosed once pupillary block has been excluded. Iris bombe is the item that does not fit, because misdirection shallows the chamber uniformly, centrally as well as peripherally, whereas bombe leaves the central chamber relatively deep and is excluded outright by a patent iridotomy.

explanation: Orthophoria at distance with exophoria at near and an essentially plano refraction is convergence insufficiency, and the entire treatment strategy is to build fusional convergence. Pencil push-ups, stereograms and base-out prism exercises all load the convergence system and are legitimate orthoptic treatments. Adding plus power beyond the manifest refraction relaxes accommodation, which through the accommodative convergence relationship reduces convergence tone and makes the near exodeviation worse. Plus lenses at near are the correct tool for the opposite problem, a high accommodative convergence to accommodation ratio with esotropia at near.

Taking the option set at face value, abusive head trauma is the answer to the question these choices belong to, which is the classic infant presentation of multilayered retinal haemorrhages extending to the periphery, often with retinoschisis and perimacular folds. Valsalva retinopathy produces a single sub-internal-limiting-membrane or subhyaloid dome of blood at the macula, typically in an adult after straining. Purtscher retinopathy shows cotton-wool patches and polygonal retinal whitening around the disc after chest compression or long-bone fracture, with relatively few haemorrhages. The pattern and distribution of the haemorrhages, rather than their mere presence, is what distinguishes non-accidental injury.

explanation: Neonatal conjunctivitis presenting on day five is acquired as the infant passes through an infected birth canal, whether the organism is Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which usually declares itself at two to five days, or Chlamydia trachomatis, which typically appears from day five to fourteen. The mechanism being tested is intrapartum inoculation of the ocular surface, not transplacental spread. Vertical transmission in the sense intended by the distractor means haematogenous transplacental passage, which is how congenital syphilis, rubella and toxoplasmosis reach the fetus and which produces systemic congenital disease rather than an isolated purulent discharge. Onset within the first twenty-four hours would instead suggest chemical conjunctivitis from prophylactic drops.

Eyelid reconstruction is governed by the proportion of the lid margin lost. A defect under about one third can be closed directly, pentagon fashion, in layers, with lateral canthotomy and cantholysis added if the closure is under tension. A Tenzel semicircular rotation flap is brought in for defects of roughly one third to one half. Sharing tissue from the opposing lid, by a Hughes tarsoconjunctival flap for the lower lid or a Cutler-Beard for the upper, is reserved for defects exceeding half the lid, and it has the significant cost of occluding the eye until division, which is unjustifiable for a small defect.

A black eschar on the nose or palate with orbital involvement is angioinvasive mucormycosis until proven otherwise; the fungus invades vessel walls, produces thrombosis and the resulting infarcted tissue turns necrotic and black. This is a surgical emergency requiring urgent biopsy, systemic amphotericin B, extensive debridement and correction of the underlying ketoacidosis or immunosuppression. Staphylococcus aureus causes a purulent orbital cellulitis with abscess formation but does not produce ischaemic eschar, because it is not angioinvasive in this way. Any diabetic or immunocompromised patient with orbital cellulitis and necrotic tissue must be assumed to have mucormycosis while cultures are pending.

The septum is the anatomical boundary, and what defines postseptal disease is involvement of the orbital contents: restricted or painful eye movement, proptosis, reduced vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect, or raised orbital pressure. Limitation of ductions is therefore the discriminating sign among these options. Fever and leucocytosis are systemic inflammatory markers that occur with preseptal cellulitis as well and cannot localise the infection. Two millimetres of proptosis falls within the range of normal interocular asymmetry on exophthalmometry and is too small a difference to be relied upon, whereas any restriction of movement with pain immediately raises the diagnosis to orbital cellulitis and mandates imaging and intravenous antibiotics.

Thyroid eye disease is driven by autoantibodies directed at antigens expressed on the orbital fibroblast, principally the thyrotropin receptor with signalling cross-talk through the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor. Activation of that fibroblast leads to hyaluronan secretion, glycosaminoglycan accumulation with osmotic swelling of the extraocular muscles, and adipogenesis in the orbital fat. This shared autoantigen between thyroid and orbit is what explains why the orbit is targeted in Graves disease, and it is the rationale for receptor-directed therapy. There is undeniably a cell-mediated component, with T lymphocyte and macrophage infiltration of the orbit, so option A is not wholly false, but the autoantigen on the fibroblast is the mechanism the question is asking for.

Reading option B as the real stem, the question is what could have been done preoperatively to improve wound healing after blepharoplasty, and tighter glycaemic control is the answer. Hyperglycaemia impairs healing at several points: neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis are blunted, fibroblast proliferation and collagen cross-linking are reduced, and microvascular disease limits tissue oxygenation. The other modifiable factors a surgeon should address before elective lid surgery are smoking, systemic steroid use, malnutrition with low protein and vitamin C, and anticoagulation. Optimising these before the operation is far more effective than trying to rescue a dehisced or poorly healing wound afterwards.

explanation: A congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing localises to the occipital cortex, because the macular representation at the occipital pole has dual blood supply from the posterior and middle cerebral arteries and is often preserved when the posterior cerebral artery territory infarcts. Lesions of the optic radiations are typically incongruous, and temporal radiation lesions produce the classic pie in the sky superior quadrantanopia without macular sparing. Lateral geniculate lesions give incongruous and characteristically sectoral defects reflecting its dual blood supply. An optic nerve lesion produces a monocular defect with a relative afferent pupillary defect, not a hemianopia respecting the vertical midline.

Bilateral adduction deficits with a large-angle primary position exotropia constitute the wall-eyed bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia syndrome, and it requires damage to both medial longitudinal fasciculi, which is entirely expected in demyelinating disease that has already produced a unilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia. The exotropia arises because the medial rectus subnuclei lose their tonic convergence input while abduction remains intact. A combined medial longitudinal fasciculus and contralateral paramedian pontine reticular formation lesion produces the one-and-a-half syndrome, in which one eye cannot move horizontally at all and the other retains only abduction with nystagmus, a very different picture from symmetric bilateral adduction failure. Neither option involving a paramedian pontine reticular formation lesion fits a patient who can still abduct both eyes.

Reading option C as the real stem, a patient with cavernous sinus thrombosis who is not alert has presumed septic thrombosis and needs immediate broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci and anaerobes, with attention to the source, usually sinusitis or a facial or dental infection. Antibiotics are the intervention that changes mortality and must not wait for imaging or cultures beyond taking blood cultures. Anticoagulation is used by many centres and may reduce propagation of the thrombus, but the evidence is weaker, the intracranial haemorrhage risk is real, and it is never the first thing given. In a patient with declining consciousness the immediate priorities are antibiotics, airway and neurological support, and neurosurgical or ENT drainage of the source.

explanation: An optokinetic response to a rotating drum is objective proof that the visual pathway is intact enough to generate pursuit and refixation, which establishes vision of at least around 20/400 and cannot be voluntarily suppressed by most patients. That positive demonstration of function is what unmasks non-organic visual loss. A mirror test showing no movement points the other way, since a seeing patient reflexively follows their own image; absent movement is what a truly blind eye would show. Absence of a relative afferent pupillary defect in a patient claiming dense unilateral loss is a genuine and useful clue, but it is weaker evidence because bilateral symmetric disease, media opacity, amblyopia and cortical lesions can all cause visual loss without an afferent defect, so it excludes rather than proves.

With movement means the far point of the eye lies behind the examiner, so the eye is either hyperopic, emmetropic, or myopic by less than the dioptric equivalent of the working distance. A wide, bright and fast reflex indicates you are close to neutrality, and if neutrality is essentially reached with no lens in place at a fifty centimetre working distance, the gross finding of plano must have the two dioptres of working distance subtracted, giving a net refraction of minus two. This is the standard trap: forgetting to subtract the working distance leaves you reporting plano. The answer depends entirely on the working distance being fifty centimetres; at sixty-seven centimetres the answer would be minus one point five.

explanation: Correcting unilateral aphakia with a contact lens reduces aniseikonia from the roughly twenty-five percent produced by spectacles to about seven percent, which is still above the five percent threshold at which most patients become symptomatic, so residual aniseikonia with a contact lens is expected rather than unexplained. To reduce it further you overplus the contact lens and neutralise the excess with a minus spectacle lens, creating a reverse Galilean telescope in which light passes first through the minus lens and then the plus lens, producing net minification of the retinal image. That is exactly what a plus eighteen contact lens with a minus three spectacle does, and it is a recognised iseikonic technique. Option A does the reverse, shifting plus power out to the spectacle plane, which increases magnification and would make the symptoms worse.
concern: The source answer states that a contact lens does not cause aniseikonia, which is not correct as an absolute. Aphakia is a refractive rather than axial ametropia, so by Knapp's law the contact lens minimises but does not abolish the image size disparity, and the residual is typically around seven percent, well within the symptomatic range. The optical principle supporting B is the reverse Galilean telescope: a plus lens at the corneal plane combined with a minus lens at the spectacle plane, separated by the vertex distance, minifies the image. I acknowledge the source's practical objection that the combination can be poorly tolerated, which is why an intraocular lens or secondary implant is usually the definitive answer in real practice, but among the three options offered B is the optically correct manoeuvre and C is a false statement.

explanation: A cavity lined by keratinised stratified squamous epithelium and filled with lamellated keratin is the textbook histology of an epidermal inclusion or epidermoid cyst, which is by far the commonest lid cyst in a child. Keratoacanthoma also contains a central keratin plug but shows a cup-shaped crater with buttressing epidermal lips and proliferating, glassy squamous epithelium with a chronic inflammatory infiltrate at the base, and it arises in sun-damaged adult skin. Squamous cell carcinoma shows atypical squamous cells invading the dermis in irregular nests with keratin pearls and dyskeratosis, not a bland epithelial lining. The key discriminator on the slide is that the epithelial lining in an epidermoid cyst is orderly and mature, with an intact granular layer and no cytological atypia.

Mutton-fat keratic precipitates are the hallmark of granulomatous inflammation and are composed of macrophages together with the epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells they transform into, which is why they appear large, greasy and yellowish on the endothelium. Fine, small keratic precipitates by contrast are made of lymphocytes and neutrophils and signify non-granulomatous inflammation. Their presence should redirect the differential towards sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, syphilis, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease and sympathetic ophthalmia. Note that epithelioid cells are simply activated macrophages, so option D is not strictly wrong; macrophages is the more inclusive and conventionally expected answer.

Nodular basal cell carcinoma, the commonest periocular skin malignancy and the commonest type of basal cell carcinoma, presents clinically as a pearly, raised papule with rolled telangiectatic borders and often central ulceration, so that is what the patient would have shown before biopsy. Histologically it corresponds to nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artefact from the surrounding stroma. Chronic keratoconjunctivitis is a red herring; its common causes are chlamydial infection, trachoma, molluscum and topical medication toxicity, and it is not a precursor to basal cell carcinoma. Other clinical red flags for a lid malignancy are madarosis, distortion of the lid margin architecture and a non-healing ulcer.

If the slide shows keratin pearls, that is squamous cell carcinoma: invasive nests of atypical squamous cells with intercellular bridges and concentric whorls of keratinisation extending into the dermis. Basal cell carcinoma would instead show basaloid nests with peripheral palisading and a cleft between tumour and stroma, and no keratin pearls. Seborrhoeic keratosis is a benign acanthotic proliferation with horn cysts and no invasion or atypia, and sebaceous carcinoma shows foamy, lipid-laden cytoplasm with pagetoid spread into the overlying epithelium and is best identified with a lipid stain on fresh tissue. Clinically an ulcerated lower lid mass is more often basal cell carcinoma, so this item is decided by the histology, not the location.
concern: The answer depends entirely on a pathology slide that is not available to me. The stem describes only an ulcerated lower lid mass, which on frequency alone would favour basal cell carcinoma; I am agreeing with A on the strength of the source's description of keratin pearls, which cannot be independently verified here.

explanation: Unaffected parents with an affected child indicate that both parents are carriers, which is autosomal recessive transmission, giving each subsequent sibling a one in four recurrence risk. The affected relative on the paternal side argues against X-linked recessive inheritance, in which affected males cluster on the maternal side through carrier mothers. Fair skin with fine, brittle, light hair in a child fits homocystinuria, which also carries ectopia lentis, a marfanoid habitus, developmental delay and a serious thromboembolic risk, and is autosomal recessive. Fifty percent would apply to autosomal dominant disease with an affected parent, and less than one percent would suggest a sporadic or new mutation event, neither of which fits this pedigree.

Congenital syphilis produces interstitial keratitis, an immune-mediated stromal inflammation that typically declares itself between ages five and twenty with deep stromal vascularisation, and after the acute episode resolves the empty vessels persist as ghost vessels. Pseudodendrites are the hallmark of herpes zoster ophthalmicus, and to a lesser extent of tyrosinaemia type II, and are raised mucous plaques without true terminal bulbs. Pterygium is a degenerative surface change of adults with chronic ultraviolet exposure and has nothing to do with syphilis. Enlarged corneal nerves point to multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B, and also occur in leprosy, keratoconus, neurofibromatosis and Fuchs dystrophy.

Autosomal dominant is the correct default for the great majority of corneal dystrophies, including the epithelial basement membrane, Reis-Bucklers, Thiel-Behnke, granular, lattice types I and II, Fuchs endothelial and posterior polymorphous dystrophies, so it is the safest answer for a picture-based inheritance question in this section. The recognised autosomal recessive exceptions are macular corneal dystrophy and congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy type 2. Y-linked inheritance does not occur in any recognised ocular disease and can always be eliminated. Mitochondrial inheritance would point to Leber hereditary optic neuropathy or a chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia syndrome, and X-linked dominant to conditions such as incontinentia pigmenti or Alport syndrome, none of which is a corneal picture.
concern: This item is unanswerable as recalled. The stem refers to the same picture as the preceding question, but that question concerns congenital syphilis, an acquired infection with no mode of inheritance, so the cross-reference is broken. My answer rests on the general prior that corneal dystrophies are autosomal dominant, not on the actual image.

explanation: Myopic laser refractive surgery flattens the central anterior cornea, but keratometers and optical biometers measure only the anterior surface and then infer total corneal power from a fixed anterior-to-posterior ratio that is no longer valid after ablation. This causes the measured keratometry to overestimate the true corneal power, so the intraocular lens formula recommends a lens that is too weak, and the eye ends up hyperopic. The remedy is to use post-refractive formulas or historical data methods rather than a standard formula on raw keratometry. Cystoid macular oedema is a general risk of cataract surgery and is not specifically increased by prior laser in situ keratomileusis, and a myopic surprise is what follows previous hyperopic ablation or radial keratotomy in some cases.

Mooren ulcer is an autoimmune peripheral ulcerative keratitis in which the adjacent limbal conjunctiva harbours the plasma cells, collagenases and proteases driving the melt, so excising a strip of perilimbal conjunctiva adjacent to the ulcer removes the inflammatory source and is the standard next step when topical and systemic immunosuppression fails. Penetrating keratoplasty during active disease is poorly tolerated and the graft will melt at its periphery; it is reserved for perforation or imminent perforation, and even then a tectonic patch graft is usually preferred. Limbal stem cell autograft is the treatment for limbal stem cell deficiency, a different problem entirely. Systemic antifungals have no role, as Mooren ulcer is a diagnosis of exclusion made only after infection and systemic vasculitis have been ruled out.

Conjunctival autograft gives the lowest recurrence rate after pterygium excision, typically in the single digits, with an excellent safety profile because the tissue is the patient's own. Bare sclera closure alone has the highest recurrence, commonly reported between thirty and eighty percent, and is now considered substandard. Mitomycin C lowers recurrence but carries a real risk of scleral melt, calcific plaque, delayed epithelial healing, infection and even perforation, sometimes years afterwards, so it fails the complications half of the question. Amniotic membrane is a reasonable alternative when the conjunctiva must be preserved for future glaucoma surgery or when the defect is very large, but its recurrence rate is consistently higher than autograft in comparative studies.

Discrete round subepithelial infiltrates in the inferior periphery, separated from the limbus by a clear zone, are staphylococcal marginal keratitis, a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to staphylococcal cell wall antigen rather than an infection of the cornea itself. The lesion sits where the lid margin makes contact, so the examination finding to hunt for is blepharitis, with collarettes, telangiectasia of the lid margin and meibomian gland dysfunction; treating the lids is what prevents recurrence. Pterygium is a fleshy limbal encroachment on the horizontal meridian, not a set of round infiltrates. Cicatricial conjunctivitis would show fornix shortening and symblepharon and points to mucous membrane pemphigoid or Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and madarosis is a sign of lid malignancy or chronic lid disease rather than the cause of these infiltrates.

The most likely underlying question, given the option set of onset intervals and the position of this item, is the timing of gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum, which classically presents at two to five days of life with a hyperacute purulent discharge, marked lid oedema and chemosis, and a real risk of corneal perforation. Onset in the first twenty-four hours suggests chemical conjunctivitis from prophylactic drops, and onset from about day five to fourteen suggests chlamydial inclusion conjunctivitis. That contrast in timing is the standard teaching point and matches the keyed answer.

explanation: The defining feature of ectopia lentis et pupillae is that the pupil and the lens are displaced in opposite directions, so pupils displaced superotemporally must be accompanied by lenses displaced inferonasally. The condition is autosomal recessive, bilateral, and typically accompanied by small, slit-shaped, poorly dilating pupils, iris transillumination defects, persistent pupillary membrane remnants, enlarged corneal diameter and axial myopia. Recognising the opposite-direction rule is what separates it from isolated ectopia lentis. Distinguish it also from simple ectopia lentis, and from the ectopia lentis of Marfan syndrome, which is superotemporal with intact zonular fibres and a normally positioned pupil.

In a mature white cataract there is no red reflex to give the surgeon a contrast background, so trypan blue stains the anterior capsule and makes the edge of the tear visible throughout the manoeuvre, which is the single most useful step for a controlled capsulorhexis. A continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis is not contraindicated; it is more important than usual because these lenses are difficult and a torn capsule is disastrous, and the intumescent white cataract needs the capsule decompressed first to prevent the tear running out radially, the Argentinian flag sign. Neither forceps nor cystotome is mandated, and both are used routinely according to surgeon preference. A deliberately small capsulorhexis is counterproductive in a dense lens, making nuclear delivery harder and predisposing to capsular phimosis.

In sickle cell disease intraocular pressure governs management of traumatic hyphema, because erythrocytes sickle in the hypoxic and acidotic environment of the anterior chamber, obstruct the trabecular meshwork disproportionately to the size of the hyphema, and the sickled cells also compromise perfusion of the optic nerve head and retinal circulation. These patients tolerate raised pressure very poorly, so the threshold for surgical evacuation is much lower, often around twenty-four to thirty mmHg sustained, rather than the higher figures used in non-sickling patients. It also dictates which drugs are safe: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors promote sickling through systemic acidosis and haemoconcentration, and hyperosmotics carry the same risk. Visual acuity is important but does not drive the surgical decision, and ultrasound is useful for the posterior segment view but is not what determines urgency here.

Maps, dots and fingerprints describe epithelial basement membrane dystrophy, in which a thickened, redundant and abnormally deposited basement membrane fails to anchor the epithelium properly through its hemidesmosomes, so the classic complication is recurrent corneal erosion with pain on waking. Reduced vision and haze can occur if the maps involve the visual axis and produce irregular astigmatism, but that is a much less characteristic and less frequently tested association. Thinning and protrusion describes keratoconus or pellucid marginal degeneration, an entirely different structural disease of the stroma. The practical point is that patients with this dystrophy should be identified before refractive surgery and before any procedure that debrides epithelium.

A corneal suture flattens the cornea along the meridian in which it lies and steepens the meridian ninety degrees away, and the magnitude of that effect increases with the length and depth of the bite. Near the visual axis you therefore want short bites placed close together, so that each suture exerts a small flattening effect and the wound is secured by numbers rather than by tension. Peripherally, longer and more widely spaced sutures are acceptable because their distorting effect on the central cornea falls off with distance. Long, widely spaced central sutures would produce marked central flattening and irregular astigmatism precisely where it damages vision most.

Arcus is normally a bilateral and symmetric age-related lipid deposition, so unilateral arcus is a vascular sign rather than a lipid sign: reduced ocular perfusion on one side prevents lipid delivery and deposition, so the arcus is characteristically absent on the side of the carotid stenosis and present on the normal side. Asymmetry therefore prompts carotid imaging rather than a serum lipid panel. A fasting lipid profile is the right investigation for bilateral arcus in a patient under about forty-five, where it may indicate familial hypercholesterolaemia. In an elderly patient with symmetric arcus no investigation is needed at all, as it is simply arcus senilis.

Feathery, fluffy infiltrate margins with satellite lesions and an endothelial plaque are the signature of filamentous fungal keratitis, and Fusarium is the classic organism, particularly after vegetable matter trauma or contact lens use. Fusarium is also the fungus notorious for penetrating deeply, traversing intact Descemet membrane to reach the anterior chamber, which is why it is so difficult to eradicate and why deep infection may need intrastromal or intracameral therapy. Candida is a yeast that causes a more discrete, suppurative, plaque-like infiltrate typically in a compromised ocular surface. Pseudomonas produces a rapidly liquefying, mucopurulent ulcer with a ground-glass surround in a contact lens wearer, and Acanthamoeba gives pain out of proportion to signs with radial keratoneuritis and a later ring infiltrate.
concern: The phrase penetrates the intact corneal epithelium is a slightly awkward recall; that description is classically applied to Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Haemophilus and Listeria, whereas fungi usually require an epithelial breach. The feathery margins make Fusarium the intended answer regardless, and Fusarium is the organism associated with penetration of intact deep corneal barriers.

explanation: When a post-traumatic ulcer fails to yield an organism on scraping, the usual reason is that the pathogen is deep in the stroma, beyond the reach of a superficial scrape, which is typical of fungi, Nocardia, atypical mycobacteria and Acanthamoeba. Corneal biopsy provides full-thickness tissue for histology, special stains and culture and is the correct next step in a non-resolving culture-negative ulcer; confocal microscopy is a useful non-invasive adjunct where available. Starting topical or systemic steroids without a diagnosis is dangerous, because steroids will accelerate a fungal or amoebic infection dramatically. Viral culture is a low-yield shot in the dark for an ulcer following trauma, and would not be the next step ahead of obtaining adequate tissue.

Ten dioptres of myopia on a cornea that is already flat at thirty-nine dioptres would leave a postoperative keratometry in the low thirties, well below the accepted floor of about thirty-four dioptres, producing an oblate cornea with poor optical quality, glare, halos, loss of contrast sensitivity and a very small effective optical zone. Corneal thickness is not the only limit on candidacy; the resulting curvature matters just as much, and a flat starting keratometry compounds the problem. Whether you treat the manifest or the cycloplegic refraction is irrelevant once the patient fails the curvature criterion. The appropriate discussion with this patient is about a phakic intraocular lens rather than a corneal ablation.

Corneal blood staining is an absolute indication for surgical evacuation, and in a child it is doubly urgent because the resulting stromal opacity clears extremely slowly, over months to years, and will cause dense deprivation amblyopia during the critical period. A total or near-total hyphema with uncontrolled pressure is itself an indication for washout, so both criteria are met here. Continued medical management risks optic atrophy and permanent corneal opacification. The usual operative approach is anterior chamber washout with a limbal paracentesis and irrigation, taking care to avoid disturbing a clot adherent to the iris and provoking rebleeding.

Herpes simplex stromal keratitis without ulceration is an immune-mediated stromal inflammation rather than active epithelial viral replication, so the treatment is topical corticosteroid to suppress the stromal immune response, always under systemic antiviral cover to prevent reactivation of epithelial disease. Oral aciclovir is preferred to topical trifluridine for that cover because trifluridine is epitheliotoxic and cannot be used for the weeks or months a steroid taper requires. Topical trifluridine alone treats epithelial dendritic disease and does nothing for stromal inflammation. Trifluridine plus oral aciclovir duplicates antiviral therapy while omitting the steroid that actually treats the stromal disease, and would leave the cornea to scar.

The excimer laser works by photoablative decomposition: high-energy ultraviolet photons break intramolecular carbon-carbon bonds directly, so tissue is removed molecule by molecule rather than by heat, which is why the cut edge is so precise. It is an argon-fluoride excimer at one hundred and ninety-three nanometres, not a combination of argon and neon lasers and not two hundred and fifty nanometres. Because the mechanism is non-thermal and the absorption at that wavelength is very high, damage to adjacent tissue is minimal, on the order of a fraction of a micron, which is exactly the opposite of option D. That short wavelength also means the radiation is absorbed superficially and does not reach the lens or retina.

Superior, and typically superotemporal, lens dislocation with intact stretched zonules is the pattern of Marfan syndrome, and the finding that must be actively excluded because it is life-threatening is aortic root dilatation with the risk of dissection; every such child needs echocardiography and cardiology referral. Homocystinuria, the main alternative, classically dislocates the lens inferonasally with disintegrated zonules and carries the risks of thromboembolism, particularly under general anaesthesia, together with developmental delay. Musculoskeletal abnormalities are certainly present in Marfan syndrome but are also present in the marfanoid habitus of homocystinuria, so they do not discriminate and they are not what changes management. The teaching point is that the direction of dislocation is the discriminator, and the answer is the systemic finding that carries the greatest risk.
concern: The stem's mention of poor school performance pulls towards homocystinuria, which would make intellectual disability or thromboembolism the answer, and this is presumably why the source is undecided between A and C. The recalled superior dislocation is the stronger clue and points to Marfan syndrome; reduced vision from a subluxed lens is itself a sufficient explanation for poor school performance.

explanation: A foamy, triangular, keratinised patch on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva is a Bitot spot, the ocular signature of vitamin A deficiency, and it is accompanied by severe surface dryness, conjunctival and corneal xerosis, night blindness and in advanced cases keratomalacia. Since vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin absorbed in the terminal ileum, the surgical history to expect is bowel resection or another cause of fat malabsorption such as bariatric surgery, cystic fibrosis, cholestatic liver disease or chronic pancreatitis. Renal transplantation is associated with immunosuppression-related infection and with steroid-induced cataract or glaucoma, not with vitamin A deficiency. Pituitary surgery would raise the question of a chiasmal field defect or of diabetes insipidus, neither of which produces conjunctival xerosis.

Hypotony is the commonest early complication of glaucoma drainage device surgery, and this eye is at particular risk because it is both vitrectomised and aphakic or pseudophakic with an open posterior segment, so there is nothing to restrict flow once the tube is patent. The consequences are a flat chamber, choroidal effusion, hypotony maculopathy and corneal decompensation, which is why non-valved devices are ligated or stented and valved devices are chosen when early flow must be limited. Tube blockage does occur, and in an eye previously filled with silicone oil residual emulsified droplets can occlude the tube, which is the reason many surgeons place the tube inferiorly in these eyes since oil floats. Suprachoroidal haemorrhage is a feared but uncommon complication, and malignant glaucoma is rare in a vitrectomised eye because the vitreous scaffold for aqueous misdirection has largely been removed.

Reading option A as cycloplegia, initial management of aqueous misdirection is medical: atropine to tighten the zonule and pull the lens-iris diaphragm posteriorly, aqueous suppressants to reduce inflow, and hyperosmotic agents to shrink the vitreous. Miotics are actively contraindicated because they relax the zonule and rotate the ciliary body forward, worsening the block. Neodymium-YAG disruption of the anterior hyaloid, which is effective mainly in pseudophakic eyes and often done through an existing iridotomy, and pars plana vitrectomy with hyaloidozonulectomy and iridectomy are the definitive steps taken only when medical therapy fails. Note that recurrence is common after medical therapy alone, so atropine is often continued indefinitely.
concern: Option A is abbreviated as Cyclo, which I have read as cycloplegic. If it were intended to mean cyclophotocoagulation the answer would be wrong, since cyclodestruction is not initial therapy for aqueous misdirection.

explanation: The nomenclature is counterintuitive: a fornix-based flap has its conjunctival incision at the limbus with the flap hinged in the fornix, and a limbal-based flap has its incision eight to ten millimetres back with the flap hinged at the limbus. Because the fornix-based suture line sits anterior to the scleral flap, aqueous is directed posteriorly and the result is a lower, more diffuse bleb, which is exactly what option D states and is why fornix-based blebs are less likely to be thin, cystic and leaking in the long term. Limbal-based flaps have their scar posterior to the scleral flap, which tends to funnel filtration anteriorly and produce a higher, more localised bleb. Option A is inverted, since early wound leak is commoner with the fornix-based incision at the limbus, and option B is inverted too, as the fornix-based approach gives better exposure and is technically easier.

Topiramate causes an idiosyncratic sulfa-related ciliochoroidal effusion that rotates the ciliary body forward, producing bilateral acute angle closure with a myopic shift, ocular pain and blurred vision, typically within the first two weeks of starting the drug or after a dose increase. Because the mechanism is not pupillary block, laser iridotomy does not help; treatment is to stop the drug and use cycloplegia and aqueous suppressants, avoiding miotics. The bilateral and simultaneous nature of the attack in a young patient is the clue that separates it from primary angle closure. Verapamil, naproxen and gabapentin are not associated with this syndrome, and it is worth remembering that other sulfa-derived drugs such as acetazolamide, hydrochlorothiazide and sulfamethoxazole can do the same thing.

Sturge-Weber syndrome carries a diffuse choroidal haemangioma and abnormal, engorged episcleral and choroidal vessels with raised episcleral venous pressure, so any rapid decompression of the globe during filtering surgery risks massive choroidal effusion or expulsive haemorrhage. This is the specific intraoperative danger, and it is mitigated by prophylactic posterior sclerotomies, slow controlled decompression, tight flap sutures and careful pressure management. Hyphema, tube exposure and flap leak are general complications of glaucoma surgery and are not particularly increased in this syndrome. The other clues in the vignette, a port-wine stain in the trigeminal distribution and an enlarged cornea from early-onset glaucoma, identify the diagnosis before you even consider the surgical risk.

Goldmann applanation works on the Imbert-Fick principle, flattening a fixed corneal area of 3.06 millimetres diameter, at which point the force required equals the intraocular pressure in convenient units; that flattening displaces roughly half a microlitre of aqueous, which is small enough not to alter the pressure being measured. The statement about astigmatism is garbled, but the real rule is that with more than three dioptres of corneal astigmatism the reading is inaccurate and the prism must be rotated so the red mark aligns with the negative cylinder axis, or two readings ninety degrees apart are averaged, rather than the test being abandoned. Applanation is affected by central corneal thickness, corneal oedema, corneal scarring and a thick tear film, which are the practical sources of error to remember.
concern: This item as recalled has two defensible answers. Option C, that applanation is not affected by scleral rigidity, is also a standard true teaching point, since minimal volume displacement makes Goldmann essentially independent of ocular rigidity in contrast to Schiotz indentation tonometry. Option A is unrecoverable but appears to refer to the half-microlitre of displaced aqueous, which would also be true. I am recording agreement with the source but the item cannot be cleanly resolved as written and should be verified against the original paper.

explanation: Phacolytic glaucoma occurs when high molecular weight lens proteins leak through an intact but hyperpermeable capsule of a mature or hypermature cataract, and macrophages engorged with that protein obstruct an anatomically open angle, producing acute pain and a very high pressure. The chamber shows cells and flare, sometimes with iridescent particles, but characteristically no keratic precipitates and no synechiae, which fits this description precisely. Phacoantigenic uveitis requires a breach of the lens capsule, usually after trauma or surgery, and produces a granulomatous zonal inflammation with mutton-fat keratic precipitates. Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis gives stellate keratic precipitates with heterochromia and no pain, and Posner-Schlossman produces recurrent painless pressure spikes without a mature cataract. Definitive treatment is prompt cataract extraction after the pressure is medically controlled.

Raised pressure at around eight weeks after a drainage device is the hypertensive phase, produced by a maturing fibrous capsule around the plate that increases resistance to aqueous absorption; it is commonest with valved implants and often settles partially over months with aqueous suppressants, needling or, if refractory, capsule excision. Steroid response usually appears within a few weeks of intensive topical steroid and resolves when the drug is withdrawn, and it is diagnosed by that temporal relationship. Persistent inflammation would be visible as cell and flare at the slit lamp. Progressive glaucoma refers to worsening optic neuropathy over years and does not account for a pressure rise in an eye with a patent drain at eight weeks.

Once the iridotomy is documented as patent, pupillary block is excluded, so iris bombe is the improbable finding and pursuing it adds nothing. Ultrasound biomicroscopy is the key investigation, showing anteriorly rotated ciliary processes with the lens-iris diaphragm displaced forward and no supraciliary effusion, which confirms aqueous misdirection. B-scan remains necessary to exclude a suprachoroidal haemorrhage or serous choroidal detachment, both of which can present identically with a shallow chamber and raised pressure after surgery. The diagnostic hallmark distinguishing misdirection from pupillary block is uniform shallowing of both the central and peripheral chamber in the presence of a patent iridotomy.
concern: The wording improbable to help in the diagnosis is ambiguous. Read literally, option D, topical and oral antiglaucoma medications, is therapeutic and contributes nothing to diagnosis, which would make D the answer. Read as which finding is improbable, the answer is A, which is what the source keys and which I have followed. Note also that the source keys the near-identical 2022 item (promotion-2022#28) as B, so the two entries are internally inconsistent.

explanation: Aqueous misdirection shallows the entire anterior chamber uniformly, centrally as well as peripherally, because aqueous is being diverted posteriorly into or behind the vitreous and the whole lens-iris diaphragm is pushed forward. That uniform central shallowing in the presence of a patent iridotomy is the diagnostic hallmark. Iris bombe belongs to pupillary block, in which the peripheral iris bows anteriorly around a pupil sealed by posterior synechiae while the central chamber stays comparatively deep, and it is relieved by iridotomy. The other conditions to exclude before settling on this diagnosis are suprachoroidal haemorrhage and choroidal effusion, both of which also present with a shallow chamber and raised pressure and are distinguished on B-scan.
